blocks.text: Not every unusual number in a dataset is wrong. A missing value is a hole, and an invalid value is one that cannot exist at all, like a negative age or a birth date set in the future. An outlier is different from both of those: it is a value that is entirely plausible in principle, just unusually far from the rest of the data. A salary of two million dollars is not impossible the way a negative age is, it is just rare. Deciding whether a rare value like that is genuine signal worth keeping, or noise worth correcting, is a real judgment call, not something a formula can settle on its own.
1. What Is an Outlier, Precisely

An outlier is an observation that deviates markedly from the other observations in a dataset. That deviation can come from two very different places, and the statistics alone cannot tell you which one you are looking at.

items: A genuine rare event: a legitimate very high income earner in a dataset of salaries, an unusually long hospital stay for a real medical reason, a real spike in traffic during a viral event.
A data error: a decimal point typo turning 4.5 into 450, a unit mismatch where one row was entered in different units than the rest, a sensor glitch producing a nonsensical spike.

blocks.text: Both cases produce the exact same statistical signature: a value far from the bulk of the data. The number itself never announces which category it belongs to. That determination has to come from domain knowledge, cross checking against other fields, or going back to the source.
2. Why the Distinction Matters

Getting this wrong in either direction has a real cost. Treat a genuine outlier as noise and remove it, and you throw away real signal, sometimes the most informative signal in the whole dataset, and can bias a model toward underestimating rare but real outcomes. Treat a data error as genuine and keep it, and it corrupts every summary statistic and every model trained on that column, since a single 450 sitting where a 4.5 belongs can drag a mean far from reality.

blocks.title: There is no automatically safe default
blocks.content: Always removing suspicious values is not the cautious choice, it is just a different way of being wrong. The only way to make an informed decision is to actually look at the flagged value in context before doing anything to it.

blocks.text: 3. The IQR Method
The interquartile range method is the classic, distribution agnostic way to flag outliers, and it is the exact technique behind a boxplot's whiskers.
Q1 is the 25th percentile of the data and Q3 is the 75th percentile. The IQR is simply the distance between them:
A value is flagged as an outlier if it falls outside these bounds:

code.content:
Lower bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
Upper bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR

blocks.text: The 1.5 multiplier is a convention, not a law of nature. Tightening it to 3 instead of 1.5 is common when you only want to flag truly extreme values rather than everything sitting past the edge of the typical range.
3.1 Why This Is the Boxplot's Whiskers

A boxplot draws its box from Q1 to Q3, and its whiskers extend out to the most extreme point still inside the 1.5 times IQR bounds. Any point beyond that gets drawn as an individual dot, and that dot is precisely what this method flags.
4. The Z-Score Method
The Z-score method asks a different question: how many standard deviations away from the mean is this value?
A common convention flags anything with an absolute z-score beyond 3, meaning it sits more than 3 standard deviations from the mean.

blocks.title: This method assumes roughly normal data
blocks.content: The 3 standard deviation convention comes from the normal distribution, where being that far from the mean is genuinely rare. On a skewed or heavy tailed distribution the same threshold can flag far too much or far too little. Worse, the outlier itself is part of the calculation: an extreme value pulls the mean toward it and inflates the standard deviation, which can shrink its own z-score back toward the cutoff. A method meant to detect the outlier ends up being distorted by the very thing it is trying to detect.

blocks.text: 5. Worked Example: An Income Column

Take a small dataset of ten annual incomes, in thousands of dollars, already sorted: 40, 42, 45, 47, 48, 50, 52, 55, 58, 500. Nine of these look like an ordinary income distribution, and one, 500, is a clear extreme value.
5.1 Computing IQR Bounds by Hand

With these 10 sorted values, Q1 falls a quarter of the way into the list and Q3 falls three quarters of the way in. Interpolating between the two nearest values gives Q1 equal to 45.5 and Q3 equal to 54.25.
Every value from 40 through 58 sits comfortably inside 32.375 and 67.375. Only 500 falls outside the upper bound, so the IQR method flags exactly one value, the one that actually looks wrong.
5.2 The Same Data with Z-Scores
The mean of this dataset is 93.7 and the population standard deviation is about 135.5, both dragged upward by the single 500.

Notice the z-score for 500 lands at only about 3.00, barely across the common cutoff, even though 500 is roughly ten times larger than every other value in the column. That is the self distortion problem from the note above playing out with real numbers: the outlier inflated the very standard deviation being used to judge it.
5.3 The IQR Calculation in Pandas

code.content:
import pandas as pd

income = pd.Series([40, 42, 45, 47, 48, 50, 52, 55, 58, 500])

q1 = income.quantile(0.25)
q3 = income.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1

lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

is_outlier = (income < lower_bound) | (income > upper_bound)
print(income[is_outlier])
# 9    500
# dtype: int64

blocks.text: 5.4 The Z-Score Calculation in Python
scipy.stats.zscore computes this in a single call, using a population standard deviation by default. The same thing can also be written out manually with the formula from section 4.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

z_scores = stats.zscore(income)
is_outlier = np.abs(z_scores) > 3
print(income[is_outlier])
# 9    500
# dtype: int64

# the same result written manually, no scipy dependency needed
z_manual = (income - income.mean()) / income.std(ddof=0)

blocks.text: Both methods agree on this particular dataset, but they will not always agree, especially on skewed columns where the normality assumption behind the z-score breaks down.
6. Visualizing Outliers

Boxplots and scatter plots are the standard visual tools for spotting outliers. A boxplot shows the IQR bounds directly as whiskers, with any point beyond them drawn individually. A scatter plot makes a single far flung point visually obvious against the rest of the cloud. This lesson focuses on the programmatic detection covered above, the full set of visualization techniques, including how to build and read these plots, is covered in the sibling Data Visualization course.
7. Handling a Flagged Outlier
Detecting a flagged value is only half the job. What you do with it depends entirely on whether you have concluded it is an error or a genuine rare event.
7.1 Removing It

Dropping the row outright is appropriate only when you are confident the value is an error and there is no way to correct it, for example when the original source is unavailable to verify a suspected typo. Removing a value you have not actually investigated is just guessing with extra steps.
7.2 Capping, or Winsorizing

Winsorizing caps a flagged value at the nearest acceptable boundary instead of deleting the row, so a value above the upper bound gets pulled down to the upper bound itself. This is a middle ground: the row stays in the dataset with all its other columns intact, but its extreme influence on statistics like the mean gets limited.
7.3 Transforming the Column

A log transform, or a similar transform such as a square root, shrinks the relative distance between extreme values and the rest of the column without touching any individual row. A value of 500 sitting next to a cluster around 50 looks far less extreme once both are log transformed, because the transform compresses large numbers proportionally more than small ones.
7.4 Leaving It and Choosing a Robust Model

Sometimes the right move is to not touch the data at all, and instead pick a modeling technique that is naturally robust to outliers. Tree based models like decision trees and random forests split on thresholds rather than computing means and variances, so a single extreme value has far less power to distort the result than it would in a linear model.

blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes
Two mistakes come up constantly.

items: Mechanically removing every statistically flagged value without ever checking whether it makes real world sense. A statistical outlier and a data error are not the same thing, treating them as interchangeable throws away legitimate rare events.

Applying the Z-score method to a heavily skewed distribution. The normality assumption behind the 3 standard deviation convention does not hold on skewed data, and the result is a set of flags that has little to do with which values are actually unusual.

blocks.text: 9. A Closing Checklist
A short checklist for approaching outliers without going on autopilot:

items: Run a detection method, IQR or Z-score, to get a candidate list. Do not eyeball the raw column and guess.
Look at each flagged value in context before deciding anything, and check the original source if you can.
Ask whether it is more plausible as a genuine rare event or as an error, and be honest that this is a judgment call.

Match the handling technique to that judgment: remove only confirmed errors, cap or transform when you want to limit influence without deleting information, and consider a robust model when you are unsure.
Document what you did and why, since the next person working with this data will need to know an outlier decision was made at all.
